text:
i just moved from 3080TI to 5080. I agree that DLSS and FSR are spotty at best and each sim needs to be adjusted to find proper AA Settings. In ACC they ruin game, graphics and smoothness, but with correct AA chosen, game is absolutely breathtaking with 50 car fields in VR, Not pushing system at all. ACC Shows I'm pushing my Rift to 3400x3800 res in headset, and its just so satisfying to play VR without any fiddling, just Go. (After turning graphics to highest setting and finding proper AA - This is only done once, then just enjoy.) DLSS actually looks good on F123, never seen FSR or FSR2 look good on any sim.

F123, AMS2 and WRC are so easy to push at 100% Epic. You can look a mile in distance, zero redraw or building in as you move, seeing stuff never knew was in game. Brilliant. Project Cars 2 is now unreal, physics as good as anything with proper power behind it. Totally blown away as removed PC2 years ago for horrible physics.

I run super sampling in OTT at 1.4 to 1.8. Everything is absolute silky smooth in VR. Loaded 400GB of Flight Sim yesterday...oh freaking hell. its real in VR now.  I can't comment on 4 series cards, but my 5080 with Ryzen 9800 hasn't been pushed yet, no OCing needed. But have 10 fans and serious water cooling. Heat is #1 issue in any intense use of cpu and gpu, it has to go. If feel it starts great and then not as good, HEAT is causing system to throttle back power....Keep a good check on Fans and Heat...most fans come to conservatively set for VR, Turn them up to come on earlier, huge effect noticed immediately.

I am heavy user of Music, Video and Photo editing, Davinci Resolve loves this power, cut processing time by 2/3s. 
It's transformed my VR Gaming and business needs, I could not be happier.

text:
I feel like this is because games aren't requiring faster data speeds..... they're requiring more data at once, per transfer. Software is outpacing elements of hardware in relation to the system as a whole. Look at the one spec that sets the 4090/5090/7900XTX apart from the rest.... Bus size. I feel like we've reached the limit for a single frame of what can be rasterized on camera given the current state of AAA optimization standards with the addition of ray tracing data. 

Were going to be forced to accept AI eventually or someone is going to have to figure out a way to greatly widen the 'freeways' on our mother boards. It almost feels like Nvidia has contracts with developers to collude. 

AMD needs to find a way to make their own mother boards with built in memory. If they can make a special CPU that can communicate with a far greater bus width in one of their GPU's.. I have a feeling it would solve the problem of low frame rates with Ray Tracing. Our bus sizes are just enough for 4k, add in Ray Tracing data and now for the complete frame, the data needs two trips for one frame. All DLSS is doing is freeing up bus space by lowering the resolution so the ray tracing data can fit across the bus at the same time as everything else and finish the frame in one trip. AMD doesn't need AI or DLSS, they can control both ends of the stick CPU - GPU. Nvidia can't. and I feel like Nvidia knows this, hence why they are locking down developers like Sony does to promote AI.. It allows Nvidia to increase frames, without destroying compatibility  raising bus speeds.. you would need proper CPU's, motherboards & memory (and probably more stuff I don't know) to do so. I think this is also why their doing this crap with TAA. It's all a solution to work around forcing people to upgrade their entire PC's with special motherboards/memory/cpu.

If the bus width is the amount of data at once (single signal) the lanes from your GPU to CPU can transfer..... I look at it like pipes with water... eventually you won't be able to increase the flow rate with pressure alone,  you would need to widen the pipes. When a single frame now requires both image rasterization data (that's now unoptimized) AND ray tracing data, you run out of room. If data is water you've now got a higher flow rate than your pipes can produce at a given width = bus width. 

To produce a frame in a way the eye sees the world, would mean to fill a bathtub all at once and every split second it took to fill from there on out was your frame rate going down.

The modern GPU is like a really big really fast ride at Disney Land, that takes waiting six hours to get on because only 30 people fit in a train and the turnstiles require a single file line.

Kena 50s 3060, 3070 80s 1440p

  4080 Forza 4080 110 fps, 4080 140 4K

Avatar 4k 50fps 4080, 4090 70

Hogwarts 4080 4k 45s, 60 4090
 
As you guys can see, I compared models directly under a higher class, as that's the only way it makes a higher class worth it since the jump will be bigger, which is why it makes no sense to compare a 4090 to a 5090 or 5080 to 4080 only 1 gen apart. text:
For readers:

General Overview
The NVIDIA RTX 5080 offers improvements over the RTX 4080 Super, with a roughly 15% performance boost in gaming for titles utilizing new features. It excels in AI tasks, provided memory demands stay under 16GB of VRAM. Despite drawing more power, it is more power-efficient and features a well-designed cooler, albeit one that adds heat to the CPU area.

However, its incremental improvements lead to many caveats, making the upgrade less compelling than expected. While 4K Cyberpunk performance is strong, bringing it close to the RTX 4090, its performance in other scenarios often falls short of expectations, even struggling to significantly outperform AMD’s 7900 XTX.

On the bright side, NVIDIA did not increase pricing, and certain niche use cases make the 5080 worth considering. AI-assisted rendering (e.g., DLSS 4 and multi-frame generation) shows potential, but their adoption in mainstream gaming remains uncertain.

Performance Breakdown
1440p Rasterization Performance
At 1440p, the RTX 5080 shows:

+20% FPS over the 4080 Super in Cyberpunk.
Noticeable uplift in Alan Wake 2, keeping 1% lows above 100 FPS.
Mediocre gains over the 7900 XTX, struggling to justify its $1,000 price.
Disappointing results in F1 24, only 7% faster than the 4080 Super and failing to surpass AMD’s older 7900 XTX.
4070 Ti Super unexpectedly looks like better value in some scenarios.
Overall: A 7-10% uplift over the 4080 Super, underwhelming for a next-gen release.
4K Rasterization Performance
At 4K resolution, improvements become slightly more apparent:

+18% over the 4080 Super, but only +10% over the 7900 XTX.
Strong showing in Cyberpunk 4K, competing with the 4090 in some scenarios.
However, in most cases, the performance uplift is marginal, reinforcing that the 5080 is “better, but not enough.”
Architecture & Hardware Changes
The 5080 brings minor architectural updates compared to its predecessor:

Still uses TSMC’s 4N process with a slight clock speed increase.
Memory upgraded to GDDR7 (16GB), but still 16GB, raising concerns for future gaming demands.
New RT cores for better ray tracing performance.
FP4-supported Tensor cores for improved AI acceleration.
AI & Ray Tracing Performance
Ray Tracing: The 5080 remains dominant, but the uplift over the 4080 Super is minor.
VRAM Issues: Certain games like Alan Wake 2 at 4K exceed 16GB VRAM usage, causing severe performance drops for cards with less memory.
NVIDIA’s AI focus: Many upgrades target AI applications, reinforcing NVIDIA’s broader business direction.
Productivity & AI Benchmarks
Blender rendering is underwhelming, but the new media engine significantly improves Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve performance, surpassing even the RTX 4090 in some cases.
AI Performance:
+20% improvement in text generation over the 4080 Super.
+16% in Stable Diffusion image generation, though 16GB VRAM remains a limiting factor.
DLSS 4 & Multi-Frame Generation (MFG)
DLSS 4 moves from CNNs to Transformer models, improving image quality at similar settings.
Multi-frame generation (MFG) can generate up to 3 synthetic frames per rendered frame, but:
High base FPS improves results, but also reduces the need for MFG.
Increases latency, meaning low-FPS games suffer more.
Performance overhead means quadrupling FPS isn’t fully realized.
Final Verdict
The RTX 5080 is a solid but underwhelming upgrade. It’s better, but not significantly so, leading to justifiable skepticism regarding its value.

Pros:
✅ 15-20% faster than the 4080 Super
✅ Better AI and productivity performance
✅ New ray tracing and neural rendering features
✅ DLSS 4 and multi-frame generation show promise

Cons:
❌ Only 16GB of VRAM, problematic for future gaming
❌ Mediocre rasterization improvements (just 10% over 7900 XTX)
❌ Multi-frame generation has trade-offs
❌ 4080 Super and 7900 XTX offer strong competition

TL;DR: The RTX 5080 is a small step forward rather than a major leap. If you already own a 4080 Super or 7900 XTX, it may not be worth upgrading.

text:
Hey, just some feedback regarding the graphs.

I think it would be nice to have a better indicator to more easily differentiate the specific card which is being reviewed, especially since this is arguably the most important part of these graphs, where the card being reviewed sits in relation to the other cards on the market. The green dot is nice, but it could still be more clear (having it be a different colour, more saturated, white border/background, etc), especially when there are multiple different cards highlighted in this way. (This goes along with the feedback which I'm sure you have seen in the other comment/s, about having the whole row highlighted to more easily see which specific card you are drawing attention to, rather than having to pan across from the dot on the right to the name on the left).

Also, I feel like having the 1% lows for every card in the fps graphs creates more clutter than it adds value to the graphs (at least for me), as in almost every case the 1% lows are roughly the same percentage lower for every card. I found myself essentially ignoring them completely, and instead mainly just looking at the overall length of the bar, which ended up just being the average because it is longer. Personally, I the main thing I gained from the 1% lows bar is the difference between the average frame rates and 1% lows for each individual card, which is good for the card being reviewed, but isn't very useful for the 3090 when the review is focused on the 5080. If there is a particular case in which the 1% lows show a significantly different story to the averages, I think it would be better to instead mention this specifically, alongside a graph displaying primarily (or only) the 1% lows. Maybe an option would by to only show 1% lows for the card in the review, which would both help differentiate the card being reviewed from the rest of the cards, remove clutter, and, in my opinion, retain the most valuable bit of information that 1% lows show (how they compare to the fps average of the card being reviewed).

Last thing, it would be nice to have some way to more easily differentiate the different generations of card. The most frequent questions I find myself asking are "how does this compare to the nvidia cards from the last generation", "how does this compare the other nvidia cards of this generation" and "how does this compare to amd". All of these would be much easier to answer if the generations were grouped in some way, maybe by saturation (have newer generations be more saturated, and the oldest be grey). You could also group manufactures by colour (red/green/blue), although then you run the risk of it looking like unicorn soup. Maybe instead you could use red/orange/yellow. It would be less clear which manufacturer is which, but I think a viewer would be able to work it out pretty quick. Maybe putting the logo of the manufacturer next to the name of the card? (I'm just realising now that you used to do this. Curious why you chose to remove it?). Not sure, just ideas.

text:
I don't know why people are specifically disappointed with the 5080. Do you guys not remember that the 4080 was 20% more expensive at launch than the 5080 was ($1200 vs $1000)? The 4080 Super was $1k at launch, but was only released a year ago, so a 15% performance increase for the same price in a year is pretty decent. The 5090 has worse value for money than the 5080 since the 5090 is about 30% faster than the 4090 in raw raster while being 30% more expensive aka 0 price/perf gains. Meanwhile, the 5080 is 15% faster than the 4080 while being 17% cheaper aka decent price/perf gains.

Also, Nvidia hasn't given up on raw raster performance forever. The 50-series Blackwell cards are using the same TSMC 5nm process that the 40-series Lovelace cards were using, so raw performance gains without the multi frame gen is not that good, but 60-series Rubin cards will be built on TSMC's 3nm process (which has a 56% higher transistor density), so the 6080 and 6090 will probably make big raster gains.

text:
It seems like we're reaching the limits of consumer graphics cards without a major breakthrough in algorithms and memory speeds as well as just the cost of memory.  At 575 Watts of power being drawn for the 5090, we're hitting a lot of practical limits.  At $15 per GB for GDDR7, that's $240 out of the price tag just for that.  It's little wonder that corporations are more focused on industrial use cases where price is less of a concern.  The math that works for lighting has a lot more value in industry.

I won't be surprised if Nintendo shifts their focus to large open worlds rather than discrete worlds and levels and focuses less on the kind of bleeding edge light rendering that these leading edge graphics cards are focused on.  The Switch 2 should be able to handle the Quest 3 for VR rendering where realistic graphics are traded for fluid and compelling worlds to explore.

text:
Horrible for us maybe, not horrible for their business since it was such a tiny percentage of their revenue and probably needed way more R&D than the cards generated.

AMD is focused on CPUs ever since Ryzen released and literally flipped the tables on Intel. That's their market competition, not NVIDIA.

And that's smart of them because NVIDIA will win that war, so why even fight it? Make some midrange stuff based on less R&D (basically just taking what was previously cutting edge) and at worst break even on GPU sales.

But again it's so heavily favored to NVIDIA. It's an almost identical situation to Intel being in like 90% of both servers AND home builds before Ryzen and Epyc.

So they don't care about GPUs anymore, unless the technology just so happens to intersect with their CPU designs (which it sometimes does).

So yeah: sucks for us as gamers, but people who build their own PCs are such a small market compared to the server space which is why NVIDIA literally doesn't give half of a crap about gamers anymore. Like at all.

AMD is almost there too. Why? Because soon you'll be running this stuff on the cloud via a thin client. For all I know the PS6 will just be a thin client that connects to an AWS system that's got 10,000 5090s in it being used for various reasons.

text:
N7 (2018 fab) cost ~10K usd per wafer, N5 (2 years later) cost ~16k usd for the same wafer. That's mass-production price, for NVIDIA their cost is higher since they use custom process. That's for a wafer of fab, not entire actual card manufacturing. Games can maintain price since nowadays they're mostly digital. But actual hardware have higher variable cost due to longer and more complex supply chain. e.g since 40 series Nvidia have to maintain 2 variant due to US ban on AI chip.

VRAM is cheap, yet AMD's sales tanked despite high praise for their N5-based RDNA3 (RX7000 series) and their abundance of VRAM compared to alternative offerings. Consumers are just picky segment, since their spending is capped by their capital surplus. AMD seems to learn and start pivoting to wider industrial user, which instead capped by ROI expectancy.

I can't believe how much of what we see on screen is no longer rendered.
If you are using path tracing, generally there is 1 light ray for every 7 pixels, or about 14.3% of the screen.
Throw in some DLSS, or other like technology and you are looking at 1/4th of the screen being generated.
You start throwing in generated frames and you can go to about 1/4.
With RTX and all DLSS features, you can be looking at 0.9% of the pixels you see on screen actually being rendered. The rest being AI estimations.

Heck, there are companies playing with trying to have every pixel AI generated.

text: It feels like it's getting to the point where having separate VRAM and system ran, with walled access separating CPU socket access (with NPU cores) from GPU core access (with Tensor Cores). There's a been a lot of talk about subjugating CPUs to the GPU, rather than the other way around, and it's become clear why. I think of it more like it's finally time colocate these, if not on package, at least in board architecture. It seems, AMD did have it right, sort of, with their old APU idea. Platforms like Steam Deck and other handhelds are showing how successful that integration can be too. So where are the desktop equivalents? Probably, stuck behind nvidia's inability to bundle x86... I wonder though, with ARM getting so fast, and the need for CPUs to be all that much faster for games in general, maybe we are at a point where nvidia can break free of that prison, and maybe that explains why they are focused on a somewhat baffling "workstation class" CPU platform? Maybe not so baffling after all.

text:
The comments here are actually brain dead 💀 like… no duh this generation “seems” like there’s not much extra performance. We’re literally reaching that point where node changes are less drastic than other generations, like the gap between the Nvidia 900 series and the Nvidia 10 series. It’s been slowly going down over time, and it’s about time people shut up and just stay with the 4080 or 4090 they probably already have :/
Plus people forget the fact game developers are becoming more and more lazy with optimizing games, that some of them require 12GBs of VRAM for 1080p, along with the new Path tracing making even a 4090 drop to its knees. Game companies are not hiring enough developers to work harder and smarter on these games to be more optimized.
It’s a double edged sword of hardware reaching the limits of actual physics, and game developers not doing enough optimization as they did compares to games released when 10 series, 16 series, and 20 series cards were available and mainstream. Sure, this series is still on that 5nm node, but would y’all really wanna see these cards double in price on a 3nm node? That node is incredibly expensive, which is why flagship Android and iPhones got a price jump when they started using that node.
Be happy the RTX5080 is less in price compared to the RTX4080 when it released. And just wait, the same generational disappointment will happen if AMD ever decides to make a new generation of GPUs, just like the difference between their RX6950XT and RX7900XTX being subpar :/

text:
Dear Linus and team… I just wanna drop a bit of love.

These interdepartmental collab videos are awesome, truly so. Sometimes, Linus isn’t the best messenger for some messages and when it comes to GPUs ( a sector once discussed on WAN show to turn more in to written format than remain on video) you really do need everyone on board fairly and genuinely represent the myriad use cases and consideration for such a piece of technology.

What keeps it fresh is that the various speakers bring THEIR expertise, and THEIR passion for that thing they do, in the name of enabling more informed purchases to be made in cool things.

Whilst passion comes in spades with Linus, the expertise… doesn’t, at least not always and so some of that passion can ring hollow as a result. He talks outside of school a lot sometimes and that’s not good for anyone. But bringing in the people who live and breathe what they get to work on at LMG, filling the gaps in Linus’ swole brain, really solves that problem.

I’m proud of you all. You were right. GPUs do get kinda stale and in terms of “every green” or “useful rather than consumable content” it’s a lot of work for the rewards. But you’ve done good here. You’ve added more flavours of communication, passion and skill set to a video, the kind that REALLY NEEDS to be dense to be useful, and using this new recipe to step forward, firing on all and everyone’s cylinders.

I really think you’re setting a new bar in product review videos with the energy and love that are put in to these efforts.

World… class.. team.

text:
The frame gen argument that you make is exactly what I've been saying. The frame gen is there to bring up frame rates that are too low, which gives a bad experience. When the frame rate is at an acceptable amount, frame gen does a good job creating those frames, but you don't need it, because it puts your frame rate above any point that you would use it.

The original DLSS was fine. Doubling your frame rate to go from 120 to 240 is fine, but not improving the raw performance because your ai "performance" is doing it for you, is the wrong route.

I refuse to put my money into Nvidia because of the ram choices. I'm not going to buy a new middle of the road GPU that barely has the needed ram to run current games. My current bottleneck on my video card is the fact that it only has 8gb of ram. The current replacement would be a 5070. At $550, it's twice as expensive as my current card cost me new. For that I'm getting a faster card, but my ram is only going up to 12gb, which is already going to be a bottleneck for some games.

Nvidia doing this is just a way to force obsolescence or if you don't want forced obsolescence, you need to buy the new flagship card that is $2000 even though it didn't make many gains from the last card.

text:
"it did NOT carry over to the lower end of the 40 series... " (Frame Gen)
Well, how could it?
FRAME GEN has a sunk processing cost. I don't know the actual numbers, but IF it took 25% of the processing budget to extrapolate a new frame, then it would take 50% of the processing budget for a card with HALF the processing power. Which leaves less processing power to generate a real frame... thus the cards that can do Frame Gen best are the higher-end cards that need it least...
That won't change until there's Frame Gen hardware that's independant of the main GPU, although improvements to the hardware and software should DECREASE the percentage hit of frame gen (and AI upscaling) as time goes on.

author: @damara2268

text: @Bunnibunnibunni  With DLSS/FSR 4 most all of the major issues have been addressed (even DLSS 3.5 is acceptable most of the time unless you have a very specific scene and you go looking). It being used currently as a crutch by some developers doesn’t change the fact that it’s still the best way forward (though I wouldn’t say a beta is much evidence of anything). The fundamental problem is hardware is and has been stalling. Process nodes are taking twice as long to develop, cost 3x more, and offer significantly less automatic performance increases compared to a decade ago. Software (and by extension AI), combined with specialized hardware, is the one area we aren’t fighting the laws of physics and the easiest place we can continue to make improvements. Nvidia, Sony and now finally AMD have all made the same bet. It’s foolish to write them off.

text:
Not defending Nvidia, but progress is being seriously hampered by improvements in the fab process. Virtually every GPU generation in history has had the benefit of being on a smaller node, bringing additional speed and improved efficiency. They are 100% at the mercy of TSMC, who has 0 additional 3nm production, leaving Nvidia stuck doing what they can with the same node. Given another year for TSMC to keep scaling up, we’d probably see a significantly improved 3nm 5000 series, but at the cost of another 12 months of waiting.

I haven’t really seen a single reviewer talk about this. While Nvidia shouldn’t have released what is essentially a refresh, that’s totally on them, but the entire hardware market is going to succumb to this new bottleneck over the coming 5-10 years. The only hope is that significant revolutions come to the shrinking process of nodes, or a new substrate is used instead of silicon. Moores Law IS dead, and this is the result.

text: I am surprised you have not talked about Moore's Law and its, uhm, pause. The reason why you are only getting 30-ish percent more performance is because they have added 30-ish percent more hardware, also why it consumes 30-ish percent more power. The current transistor size has reached the limits of sensibly priced physics. Going any smaller requires so much error checking, as the smaller you go the more quantum shenanigans you have to deal with, that it currently makes no sense to do so. As it stands, using the current large scale transistor fabrication methods Moore's Law is paused or dead, depending on who you ask. I am in the camp of paused as I have seen some very interesting developments from smaller "stealth" companies.

author: @robotovalle

text:
That's just misinformation. Generated frames go between rendered frames, and the maximum added latency is FG render time + rendered frame time, so about 35ms at 30fps. 
 It doesn't wait for multiple future frames to be rendered.

In practice, rendered frames are not displayed immediately, and this delay is deducted from FG latency. A game natively rendered~60fps see less than 10ms of added latency -- often much less (I think the average is more like 6). Native 30fps will see an average of around 10ms of latency added -- which, unless you're on triple buffered vsync or something, won't get you anywhere near to 100ms.

text: No they do not wait for two frame, it use motion vector from the game engine instead to predict the most likely next position. Then they look for the player input and use re-projection to slightly adjust the pixel position if they are too far from the expected position.  It definitively add latency but nowhere near as much as using two frames. It is also why this need to be built right into the game engine. The frame generator need to be able to access the game engine motion vector and also need access to  the player input.

text:
​@juliox9 If you're getting bottlenecked by vram you probably shouldn't buy Nvidia

They intentionally don't give you enough vram so you'll have to upgrade more often (with exception to their 16gb variants of their bottom-end cards which overspec the vram compared to the other specs, but there aren't 16gb versions offered for the cards that could actually use it).

Looking at last gen, Nvidia's 4070ti Super (16gb) and AMD's 7800XT (also 16gb) had very similar performance in native rasterized gaming - the one that did better depended on the game obviously, overall very slight edge to Nvidia, but we're comparing Nvidia's $800 model for that gen with AMD'S $500 model. If you're not buying the very top end, then unless you like Nvidia's edge in ray tracing and AI features you'll get more per dollar out of AMD, and you can expect AMD's higher end to last longer before feeling old than similarly-priced Nvidia cards.

text:
9:15 You're talking about refresh rate, not fps.
If you use any form of sync and you go near refresh rate or above it, you double the latency. If you disable all the syncs, then yeah increasing fps lowers latency, even if going above refresh rate.
Games on pc and newer haredware use frame skipping, thus you get stutters, so the latency isn't much worse compared to 30fps vs 60fps with 120hz, the higher the refresh rate, the lower the latency. In older consoles you would have no frameskipping, thus everything would slow down if fps lowers, regardless what the refresh rate was.
You should educate yourself with blurbusters gsync tests.

text:
Before now, these would have just been the refresh cards (super or Ti models et cetera) and the 5090 would have been the 4K series Titan card, the 5K series really isn't an upgrade if you have a mid to top tier 4K series card, CPU's just yet getting everything from the 4080/4090 cards as yet, not even the 9950X3D is able to push the top end 4K series with real rendered frames, so you can spend 3K and still only get 25% at best performance upgrade, the 5090 is just to CPU bound, just not worth it yet, wait until a card comes out that can push Stalker 2 max settings with a locked 240 FPS 4K raw rendering, until then a decent X3D CPU and any GPU from the GTX1080 and up is good until a worthy successor comes along.

As Linus said in this vid, this is a repeat of what Intel was doing in the CPU space when they had no real competition, they had no need to spend on R&D, and just kept re-releasing what was ultimately the same CPU every new generation of SKU's, for the longest time, many years in fact, there was no need to change your CPU from the Intel, i7 2700K & i5 2500K, there were almost no benefits for gaming, and once AMD launched the incredible Ryzen CPU's, this came back to bite Intel in the arse, in fact they are still reeling the consequences of skimping on R&D, as AMD continues to dominate them. 

The same could happen to Nvidia in the GPU space, if they carry on releasing new generations of GPU SKU's without any real next generation improvements and advancements, I really hope Intel & AMD make them regret their greed and lack of R&D spending for real tangible gaming GPU upgrades, due to Nvidia's focus on A.I., we may never see another GTX 9K or 10K quality series of GPU's from them, I hope AMD comes through with their Tri-Die & Multi-Die GPU's, and pull of a Ryzen in the GPU market, same for Intel, I hope they continue to really push things with their GPU's, they have already made huge headway with Battlemage, I wonder also, if AMD & Intel could come together to make an amazing true next gen GPU line, they could pull resources for at least one generation, to make something really special and bring serious competition to Nvidia.

text: LTT: You need to watch Sophie’s video on silicon scaling past and futures, amdahls law, economics of transistors and chips to start understanding why we ran out of steam on pure rasterization. AI is a solution to a scaling problem. Rasterization relied a lot on CPU, we hit a wall in CPU scaling (amdalhs law) to get more scaling Nvidia shifted to tile based rendering. The spent time Pershing that technique. This is coupled with ther drive to more realistic lighting that can’t be solved in classic rsdterization.  If it could unreal engine and others would be working with intel to solve it - they may already be doing this with software we have yet to see meaningful results. Short version, it’s a confluence of really hard problems to solve and a dramatic price increase in the cost per transistor to manufacture.

text:
Like, only so much can be done on the same process node at similar GPU size without the sole focus of the architecture being Shader Core Perf performance.

Nvidia rather than focusing on speeding up the shaders, focused on adding even more flexibility and capability outside of them (Completely unifying the shader's data types again to have all handle FP32/INT32 rather than half being only FP32, speeding up the Tensor Cores and making latency between them and the shaders even smaller, RT core improvements, flip metering at the hardware level, The new nvenc encoder.etc)

So improvements at the same core type are banking on scenarios where those changes, and the boost in bandwidth, can help (RT workloads predominantly. And seemingly reducing DLSS 4's cost)

text:
The fact that you instantly go to the inefficiency of modern games rather than ripping on Nvidias price points and lack of improvement is pretty sad. I get that game companies need to do better with their games, but Nvidia also needs to offer improvements on their new cards if they are going to sell them for more than the last iteration.

Part of the issue with new games is that they are being pushed to release quicker and quicker. The other issue, is that more games are having more things rendered at a time. Either through bigger open worlds, or worlds that have more objects to try to create realism. You may think that games today don't look much different than games 5-10 years ago, but we are at the point where game designers are putting more into the small things in games. In the past a small object may have just been a small noninteractive object that just did an animation. Now, each one of those tiny objects are different and interact different with the environment, and your video card needs to render each one separate. It adds up quick. It doesn't add a lot to the viewing pleasure, but if we are trying to get more realistic, it's a step that would need to happen. In the past, it wouldn't have been noticeable. Now, if you use that low poly render repeated all over the place for that object, it would look terrible, because everything around it has improved.

In short, it's been subtle changes, but those subtle changes are what really tax the video cards

text:
@Nopenotreally.  fps is not always directly linked to vram capacity. Even more so the case in most modern games. The ways ram effects frame rate is primarily 1. speed 2. misses.

to elaborate.
1) the faster the ram is the faster the chip can retrieve the data to begin its computation and continue its computation.  for ram -> CPU this is done in 64bit width. for gpu's this is somewhere between 128 - 256 bit width depending on make / model. 

meaning a GPU will pull data 128 - 256 bits at a time from the ram. if the ram is unable to keep up with the chips demand. it will drop FPS. Adding more VRAM does not change this as the GPU will still only pull at 128 - 256 bits per cycle from VRAM to the gpu's cache.

2) misses. which would be the argument for more VRAM. Unless you are doing something stupidly complex like high fidelity fluid simulation / true path tracing. there's 0 justification for this. 

if the chip asks the VRAM for something and it's not there. it has to ask the CPU to send it over. which means pulling it from system ram. God forbid it's not able to fit there and it goes to disk creating a page file. then you are REALLY waiting on it. 

More ram just means you can store more data that the scene needs to run. 

more and more games are taking the approach of "I will just load everything to VRAM so it's always there when I need it" instead of defining conditions to load things in and out and manage that memory. 

to get into further detail on how everything meshes. the CPU provides vertices. the dots of a triangle used that needs to be rendered. Then the GPU plots them on the screen, does culling, ext, paints textures. If this data was not in the VRAM is results in a miss. 

The only justifications I can see as valid reasons to need 16gb of Vram are 

A) you are doing ray tracing / fluid sims which requires the GPU to generate and store large volumes of data points for paths. 

B) you are storing somewhere around 300-400 4k textures for a scene. Which would be absolutely insane because you don't even have enough bindable slots and running that man in a bindless paradigm would be a major FPS killer. 

C) you just load all your textures to vram because gpu's have enough and you don't have to care about streaming in and out only what's needed. Which im 100% okay with, it's a manpower sink that takes away from other things. But when you don't use that manpower to improve the game but instead cut budget and team sizes. its 100% unacceptable.

text:
@DesFTW_  It's not a matter of FP4 vs FP8, it's a matter of how the ML accelerators are distributed per core. On RDNA3 they sit with the CUs and to give priority to the accelerators you need to sacrifice raster performance. RDNA4 uses a different topology do the models created for RDAN4 need to be optimized and re-adapted to RDNA3. 

The different topology is also the reason why probably FSR4 on RDNA3 will perform less tasks or use a different type of neural network entirely to do upscaling. AMD hasn't released any details for it but if it was a matter of FP8 vs FP4 instructions it would be much easier to port and would only comport a minimum performance hit with complete feature parity. Upscaling uses way less compute power than you might think.

text:
@alexkarter5854  This is the wrong way to look at it. Video cards are becoming more of a necessity, so the fact that cards are still being bought at these higher prices is less about the price being too low and more about the individuals buying them needing them.

This is a bad practice on nvidias side. They see that the old product is still selling at above price because of scalpers, so they offer the new one at a higher price and say that it's to stop the scalpers. The scalpers buy those ones and sell at a higher price, so nvidia does it again. All it is, is a big cash grab. The company doesn't need to offer much of a gain, because they are forcing demand with the lack of production.

Gone are the days of getting a mid grade video card at a reasonable price. Also gone, are the days of getting a mid grade video card and being able to run every game.

My 460 that I bought back in February of 2011 worked for years (replaced it in 2019). Towards the end of me using it, I had to lower settings, but it still worked on every flagship game. I was getting 60fps at 1080. Now, when buying a brand new 5070 (should be a step up from what the 460 was) You pay more than twice as much, and from the get go, you have too low of vram for some games  and are playing on reduced settings. You'll be lucky if 4 years down the road, the card is even usable on a flagship game.

Released in mid 2010 my non flagship 460 gtx video card was $220 and had 2gb of ram. In 2017 my $230 580RX from AMD had 8gb of ram. That's 4x the vram in 7 years for close to the same price. Here we are over 7 years later and nvidias offering of the 5070 is $550 and offers 12gb of ram. 2x the cost and only a 50% increase in ram.

I know, I'm jumping back and forth between brands, but the price was consistent across the first two and if I recall, the nvidia 1060 was clost to the same price as the rx580, but with 6gb of ram, which still shows a regression in the increase in ram, when it feels like the need for vram has went up exponentially

text: @TheArcanis87  the reason the RTX 3080 had a 320-bit interface was because it used heavily disabled GA102 dies that were also used with the 3090. Nvidia did that because they had yield issues at Samsung with GA103. With the RTX 50 series, Nvidia would have to disable over half the SMs in GB202 to make a 5080 with a wider bus. Silicon pricing is done per wafer and you can fit more GB203 dies onto a single wafer compared to GB202. Nvidia would refer to keep the most expensive GB202 silicon for the RTX 5090 and professional Blackwell cards that they can sell for more than a 5080.

text:
@Fluffball555  It has everything to do with VRAM capacity, GDDR7 WILL have 3GB and 4GB chips, GDDR6 tops out at 2GB chips. Sadly 3GB GDDR7 chips were delayed until H2 2025, so expect 5000 Super/Ti-Super cards in 2026-2027 with 18GB for 192 bit cards, 24GB for 256 bit cards and 48GB for 512bit cards(and if they release a 384 bit card 36GB).

Each VRAM chip is 32 bit wide at full bandwidth mode, meaning it takes 32 bits of the memory bus, thus a 128 bit card can have 4x chips, 256 bit can have 8x chips and 512 bit can have 16x chips running at 32 bit mode.

Some professional GPUs run their chips at 16 bit mode and thus you get twice the chips, but half the bandwidth.

And some GPUs like the 7600xt and 4060Ti 16GB have a stacked clam-shell design where they stack two chips in one slot, one on each side of the PCB, but that is expensive and requires extra cooling, tooling and config.
